# MLPL Language Reference

## Numeric Literals

```
42        # integer
-3        # negative integer
1.5       # float
-0.25     # negative float
```

Integers are sequences of digits. Floats contain a decimal point with
digits on both sides. No scientific notation.

## String Literals

```
"scatter"
"line"
"hello"
```

Double-quoted ASCII strings. Strings are a separate value kind from
arrays and are used as type-name arguments to built-ins like `svg()`.
Strings cannot be combined with numeric operators.

## Identifiers

```
x
my_var
result2
_temp
```

Start with an ASCII letter or underscore. Contain ASCII letters,
digits, and underscores. Case-sensitive.

## Builtin / Operator References (`:foo`)

```
:add
:max
:+
:*
:sigmoid
```

A first-class-ish reference to a builtin or operator. Lexed as
`:` immediately followed (no intervening space) by an
identifier-start character or one of `+ * / -`. Evaluates to a
`Value::BuiltinRef { name }`. Used as the first argument to
higher-order builtins like `reduce(:op, x[, axis])`. Lives in a
separate namespace from regular variables, so `add = 42` cannot
shadow `:add`. Variables can hold a BuiltinRef:

```
f = :max
reduce(f, [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6])    # 9
```

The annotation form (`x : [batch] = ...`) requires a space after
`:` and is unaffected. The design is forward-compatible with
first-class functions: `:foo` can lift to a function value
cleanly.

## The Three Kinds of Name: `name` vs `:name` vs `u:name`

One naming design, three deliberate roles:

| Form | What it is | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name(...)` | CALL a builtin. The bare name is only meaningful applied to arguments. | `disp(G)`, `rotate(x, 1, 0)` |
| `:name` | QUOTE a builtin into a first-class VALUE (APL's quoted function). What higher-order builtins consume; typing `:disp` alone shows the reference, not a rendering. Applying the quoted form calls it: `:disp(G)` and `disp(G)` are the same call. `:disp G` (no parens) is NOT a command -- the REPL says so. | `reduce(:add, S, 0)`, `f = :max`, `:disp(G)` |
| `u:name` | A USER-DEFINED function. The mandatory `u:` namespace prefix keeps your names from ever colliding with (or shadowing) present or FUTURE builtins -- a new builtin release can never break your workspace. | `def u:life(g) { ... }`, `u:life(G)` |

Why the trichotomy: calls and values must look different (so
`reduce(add, v)` cannot silently pass a VARIABLE named add where
a function was meant), and user space and builtin space must
look different (APL workspaces suffered decades of name-clash
pain; the `u:` prefix is the cure priced at two characters).
The quoting rule covers BOTH spaces: `:name` quotes a builtin
and `:u:name` quotes YOUR function -- a first-class reference
you can bind, store in record fields, pass, and return. A test
registry is a record of references. `call(f, args...)` invokes
either kind uniformly, with errors naming the REFERENCED
function; the Result combinators `map_ok` / `and_then` /
`or_else` take a reference as their first argument. References
identify definitions by NAME (late binding): re-defining
`u:name` means existing references call the new definition.

Introspection follows the same split: `:builtins` lists the
builtin space, `:fns` lists YOUR `u:` space, `:list u:name`
prints a definition back (verbatim source, `#` comments
included, when defined in this process), and `:describe` works
on both.

## Value Kinds

Every value the evaluator produces is one of NINE kinds (the
`kind` field connect-mode responses carry uses the same names):

| Kind | Produced by | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `array` | literals, range/fill/randn, all math | The workhorse: rank-N dense f64 tensor, optional axis labels. |
| `builtin-ref` | `:name` | The quoted-builtin value above. |
| `device-tensor` | `device("mlx"/"cuda") { ... }` results held on-device | Fetched back on demand; keeps GPU residency explicit. |
| `model` | linear/chain/attention/... model DSL | Layer tree; renders as a Sankey diagram. |
| `record` | `{field: expr, ...}` literals | Named fields, `r.field` access; the canonical error-object payload. |
| `result` | `ok(v)` / `err(e)`, to_number/to_int/env, list_get | The two-state sum consumed by is_ok/unwrap/unwrap_or/get_value/get_error/`?` (docs/error-handling.md). |
| `string` | `"..."` literals, svg()/disp() and other renderers | Separate from arrays; `x = "hi"` binds a string. |
| `string-list` | `["a", "b"]` (all-string literals), tokenizer vocab helpers | Sibling of array for text data. |
| `tokenizer` | train_bpe | Paired with apply_tokenizer/decode. |

## Array Literals

```
[1, 2, 3]              # vector (rank 1)
[[1, 2], [3, 4]]       # matrix (rank 2)
[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] # 2x3 matrix

| `:name` | QUOTE a builtin into a first-class VALUE (APL's quoted function). What higher-order builtins consume; typing `:disp` alone shows the reference, not a rendering. | `u:name` | A USER-DEFINED function. The mandatory `u:` namespace prefix keeps your names from ever colliding with (or shadowing) present or FUTURE builtins -- a new builtin release can never break your workspace. | `def u:life(g) { ... }`, `u:life(G)` |

Why the trichotomy: calls and values must look different (so
`reduce(add, v)` cannot silently pass a VARIABLE named add where
a function was meant), and user space and builtin space must
look different (APL workspaces suffered decades of name-clash
pain; the `u:` prefix is the cure priced at two characters).
The quoting rule covers BOTH spaces: `:name` quotes a builtin
and `:u:name` quotes YOUR function -- a first-class reference
you can bind, store in record fields, pass, and return. A test
registry is a record of references. `call(f, args...)` invokes
either kind uniformly, with errors naming the REFERENCED
function; the Result combinators `map_ok` / `and_then` /
`or_else` take a reference as their first argument. References
identify definitions by NAME (late binding): re-defining
`u:name` means existing references call the new definition.

Introspection follows the same split: `:builtins` lists the
builtin space, `:fns` lists YOUR `u:` space, `:list u:name`
prints a definition back (verbatim source, `#` comments
included, when defined in this process), and `:describe` works
on both.

## Value Kinds

Every value the evaluator produces is one of NINE kinds (the
`kind` field connect-mode responses carry uses the same names):

| Kind | Produced by | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `array` | literals, range/fill/randn, all math | The workhorse: rank-N dense f64 tensor, optional axis labels. |
| `builtin-ref` | `:name` | The quoted-builtin value above. |
| `device-tensor` | `device("mlx"/"cuda") { ... }` results held on-device | Fetched back on demand; keeps GPU residency explicit. |
| `model` | linear/chain/attention/... model DSL | Layer tree; renders as a Sankey diagram. |
| `record` | `{field: expr, ...}` literals | Named fields, `r.field` access; the canonical error-object payload. |
| `result` | `ok(v)` / `err(e)`, to_number/to_int/env, list_get | The two-state sum consumed by is_ok/unwrap/unwrap_or/get_value/get_error/`?` (docs/error-handling.md). |
| `string` | `"..."` literals, svg()/disp() and other renderers | Separate from arrays; `x = "hi"` binds a string. |
| `string-list` | `["a", "b"]` (all-string literals), tokenizer vocab helpers | Sibling of array for text data. |

explicitly on failure via `is_ok` / `unwrap_or` / `err_message`.

| `to_number(s)` | 1 | Parse `s` (a `Value::Str`) as an `f64`. Returns `Ok(scalar)` on success; `Err("to_number: cannot parse \"abc\" as a number")` on failure. Leading/trailing whitespace is trimmed. |
| `to_int(s)` | 1 | Parse `s` as an `i64`, rejecting non-integer numeric strings. Returns `Ok(scalar)`, `Err("to_int: \"3.5\" is not an integer")`, or `Err("to_int: cannot parse \"xyz\" as an integer")`. |
| `env(name)` | 1 | Read the OS environment variable `name`. Returns `Ok(string-value)` if set; `Err("env: NAME not set")` if unset. Pair with `unwrap_or(env(\"VAR\"), \"default\")` for a fallback. |
| `args()` | 0 | Return a `StrList` of the trailing CLI args passed to the script after the `--` separator (`mlpl-repl -f script.mlpl -- foo bar` makes this `["foo", "bar"]`). Empty list when run from the interactive REPL or the web playground. |

| `read_stdin()` | 0 | Block until EOF and return all stdin bytes as a `Value::Str`. Refuses to read from an interactive terminal: `Err("read_stdin: stdin is a terminal; pipe input or use args() instead")` when stdin is a TTY. 417:| `to_json(v[, opts])` | 1-2 | The deterministic encode half of `parse_json`, RESULT-based like it: `ok(json_string)` / `err(message)`. ## Built-in Functions

### Array Operations

| Function | Args | Description |
|----------|------|-------------|
| `argtop_k(scores, k)` | 2 | Indices of the top-`k` entries of a rank-1 `scores` vector, sorted by descending score (ties go to the lower index). Used to pick the strongest variants in ensemble / Neural-Thicket workflows. |
| `running_product(v)` | 1 | Running product along a rank-1 vector (e.g. a diffusion noise schedule's alpha-bar). `cumprod` is the deprecated alias. |
| `transpose_axes(a, perm)` | 2 | Generalized dyadic transpose (APL2's `P transpose A`): result axis `i` draws from source axis `perm[i]`, 0-based, axis labels carried along. `transpose_axes(reshape(B, [3,3,3,3]), [0,2,1,3])` re-ranks a row-major 9x9 into Sudoku's block-major layout; `disp` then renders the blocks as a boxed grid. Bad perms (wrong length, duplicate or out-of-range axes) error loudly. |
| `grade_up(v)` | 1 | Stable argsort, ascending: the index vector that sorts rank-1 `v` (ties keep original order). `gather_rows(X, grade_up(d))` reorders a dataset by difficulty -- the curriculum idiom. |
| `grade_down(v)` | 1 | Stable argsort, descending. `gather_rows(C, grade_down(scores))` ranks candidates best-first; `take(grade_down(s), 0, 0)` is the best index. |
| `call(f, args...)` | 1+ | APPLICATIVE invocation of a callable: a `:u:` reference, a builtin reference, or a partial. Supplying fewer arguments than the user function's arity returns a PARTIAL (the function plus bound arguments -- data, not a closure); exact arity executes; EXTRA arguments apply left-associatively, so `call(f, a, b, c)` is `(((f a) b) c)`. Errors identify the referent. Builtin references keep exact-arity semantics (their arity is not fixed) -- wrap one in a `u:` definition to stage it. |
| `map_ok(f, r)` | 2 | Apply `f` inside `ok(...)`: `ok(x)` becomes `ok(f(x))`; `err` passes through untouched. `f` is a function reference; builtin references need an array payload. |
| `and_then(f, r)` | 2 | Chain fallible steps (the railway): `ok(x)` becomes `f(x)` where `f` itself returns a Result; `err` passes through. |
| `or_else(f, r)` | 2 | Recover: `err(e)` becomes `f(e)`; `ok` passes through untouched. |
| `bracket(setup, use, teardown)` | 3 | Guaranteed-finally over three `:u:` references: `setup()` produces the fixture (`ok(x)` unwraps; a plain value IS the fixture; a failure skips both other hooks), `use(fixture)` runs once with hard errors captured as the structured `{kind, message}` record, and `teardown(fixture)` ALWAYS runs after a successful setup. Use's failure stays primary; a teardown failure after success is the result; when both fail the teardown diagnostic rides in the error payload's `teardown_error` field. Composes with `?`. |
| `each(f, v)` | 2 | Apply a function reference per ELEMENT of an any-rank array, shape preserved (APL2's each): `each(:u:sq, M)`. The function receives a scalar and must return one (loud error naming the index otherwise). Arithmetic already pervades whole arrays -- reach for `each` when the per-element work is a FUNCTION, not an expression. |
| `table(f, a, b)` | 3 | The outer product over `f` (APL2's jot-dot, BQN's table): rank-1 `[m]` and `[n]` inputs give the `[m, n]` matrix of `f(ai, bj)`. `table(:u:times, v, w)` is the multiplication table. |
| `atop(f, g, x...)` | 3+ | Immediate composition `f(g(x...))` (BQN's atop): `atop(:u:sq, :mean, v)` squares the mean. |
| `over(f, g, x, y)` | 4 | Immediate composition `f(g(x), g(y))` (BQN's over): `over(:u:add2, :u:sq, 3, 4)` combines the squares of both sides. |
| `tests()` | 0 | Stable names of every `@test`-annotated function as a string list, in registration (source/include-splice) order. Discovery only -- nothing is invoked. |
| `test_info(name)` | 1 | One test's registry row as a record: `{name, fn, tags, skip, expected_failure, timeout_ms, source, line}`. `fn` is the `:u:` reference, so `call(test_info(n).fn)` runs the test. Unknown names error, listing the registered tests. |
| `annotations(name)` | 1 | ALL of a definition's `@word` annotations as a record `{word: payload, ...}`; bare annotations map to scalar 1. Accepts `"u:name"` or `"name"`. The reflection door for documentation/formula metadata. |
| `expunge(name)` | 1 | Free a name from EVERY value table -- and, for a `u:` name, from the function table and the `@test` registry (APL2's quad-EX). Accepts one name string or a string list; returns 1 per name that is free afterwards (already-unbound included -- cleanup is idempotent) and 0 for a malformed spelling. The interactive form is `:erase name name...` (APL's `)ERASE`). |
| `fs_walk(root, opts)` | 2 | Sandboxed directory walk: `{recursive: 1, kind: "file"\|"dir", pattern: "test_*.mlpl"}` (simple `*` wildcard); returns `ok(list)` of root-relative paths in LEXICAL order (they feed straight into the other fs calls); symlinks are never followed. Every fs builtin resolves paths against the sandbox root (`--source-dir`, else the script directory) and answers `err(...)` -- never a hard error -- for I/O failures or traversal outside the sandbox. |
| `read_text(path)` | 1 | Sandboxed exact-text read: `ok(text)` with Unicode preserved byte-for-byte, `err(...)` otherwise. |
| `write_text(path, s)` | 2 | Sandboxed exact-text write (creates or replaces): `ok(1)` / `err(...)`. |
| `read_bytes(path[, offset, length])` | 1 or 3 | Sandboxed raw-byte read: `ok(bytes)` -- a rank-1 array of byte values (`0..256`) -- or `err(...)`. The 1-arg form reads the whole file; the 3-arg form SEEKS to `offset` and reads at most `length` bytes (clamped at EOF) WITHOUT materializing the rest, for bounded large-file analysis. `offset`/`length` are non-negative integers (a bad type is a hard error). Binary formats round-trip through `decode_bytes`/`tokenize_bytes` and `parse_json`/`to_json`: `parse_json(decode_bytes(unwrap(read_bytes(p))))`. |
| `file_size(path)` | 1 | Sandboxed byte count from file metadata (no read): `ok(count)` / `err(...)`. Pairs with the 3-arg `read_bytes` to bound and validate offsets when scanning a large file (e.g. a safetensors header). |
| `write_bytes(path, bytes)` | 2 | Sandboxed raw-byte write (creates or replaces): `bytes` a rank-`<=1` array whose cells are integers `0..=255`. Result-based for every outcome: a wrong-typed value or an out-of-range/non-integer cell is an `err(...)` naming the culprit (not a hard error), success is `ok(1)`. Store encoded data as raw bytes: `write_bytes(p, tokenize_bytes(unwrap(to_json(v))))`. |
| `append_bytes(path, bytes)` | 2 | Sandboxed INCREMENTAL byte-array append -- the bounded output sink. Appends `bytes` (a rank-`<=1` array of integers `0..=255`) to the file, creating it if absent; returns `ok(count)` / `err(...)` (invalid input is an err, like `write_bytes`). Position is `file_size(path)` and each append flushes, so a program emits output chunk-by-chunk without holding the whole result: read a slice with `read_bytes(p, off, len)`, transform, `append_bytes(out, chunk)`. |
| `write_stdout(bytes)` | 1 | Write a rank-`<=1` byte array (integers `0..=255`) to process stdout and flush -- the NON-SEEKABLE binary sink (the `ByteSink` counterpart to `read_stdin`, for pipes / stdout). Returns `ok(count)` / `err(...)` (invalid input is an err). Not sandboxed (stdout is the process's own); text goes through `tokenize_bytes`. A compiled or `-f` CLI can stream binary output: `write_stdout(unwrap(read_bytes(p, off, len)))`. |
| `write_atomic(path, value)` | 2 | Sandboxed CRASH-SAFE write: `value` a string (its UTF-8 bytes) or a byte array (as in `write_bytes`). Writes a hidden sibling temp file then `rename`s it over the target, so a concurrent reader sees the old file or the whole new one -- never a torn write (atomic on a POSIX same-filesystem rename); the temp is removed on failure. Result-based: a wrong-typed value or out-of-range byte is an `err(...)`, success is `ok(1)`. Durable persist: `write_atomic(p, unwrap(to_json(v)))`. |
| `remove_path(path)` | 1 | Sandboxed removal of a file or directory tree: `ok(1)` / `err(...)`. |
| `parse_json(s[, opts])` | 1-2 | JSON text to a typed MLPL value -- the inverse of the test-event encoding: objects become records, strings stay strings (Unicode and escapes exact, surrogate pairs included), numbers become scalars, homogeneous arrays become vectors or string lists (mixed/nested arrays are an err -- MLPL arrays are flat), `true`/`false` become 1/0, `null` becomes the empty vector. A DUPLICATE object key is an `err(...)` (last-wins overwrite would silently drop evidence -- e.g. a repeated safetensors tensor name). Returns `ok(value)` or `err(message with the byte position)`, so `event = parse_json(line)?` composes. An optional `opts` record caps decoding: `max_depth` (default 128) bounds object/array nesting -- guarding the recursive decoder against stack overflow on adversarial input -- and `max_bytes` rejects oversized input before parsing; `max_elements` caps the cumulative collection size (record fields + array cells + string-list items) after decoding. `results` (opt-in, off by default) rebuilds the Result-shaped records `to_json` emits -- `{ok, value}` with `ok == 1` back into `ok(value)`, `{ok, error}` with `ok == 0` into `err(error)`, recursively -- so a serialized `ok(x)` / `err(e)` survives the round trip: `unwrap(parse_json(unwrap(to_json(ok(5))), {results: 1}))` is `ok(5)`. (The shape is an ordinary record, hence opt-in; a genuine `{ok: 1, value: x}` data record also rebuilds under the flag.) A malformed `opts` (non-record, or a negative/non-integer field) is a hard error. Reserved `$mlpl` tagged envelopes (from `to_json(v, {tagged: 1})`) are reconstructed UNCONDITIONALLY -- a rank-`>=2` array or a Result comes back as itself -- so `parse_json(unwrap(to_json(v, {tagged: 1})))` losslessly round-trips ANY data value. |
| `to_native(v)` | 1 | Encode any DATA value to a versioned, self-describing BINARY byte array (a rank-1 `0..256` array), RESULT-based: `ok(bytes)` / `err(message)`. Header `MLPB` + version + payload length; tagged values for scalars, arrays (any rank, exact shape), strings, string lists, records (sorted keys), and `ok`/`err` Results; canonical little-endian, deterministic (equal value -> equal bytes), all numbers `f64`. Non-data kinds (models, tokenizers, ...) are an `err`. Round-trips with `parse_native`; the bytes feed straight into `write_bytes` / `write_atomic`: `write_bytes(p, unwrap(to_native(v)))`. |
| `parse_native(bytes[, limits])` | 1-2 | Decode a native (`MLPB`) byte array back into a value, RESULT-based: `ok(value)` / `err(message)`. Validates the magic, version, and payload length; rebuilds scalars, arrays (exact rank + shape), strings, string lists, records, and `ok`/`err` Results losslessly. An optional `limits` record (`max_depth`, `max_bytes`, `max_elements`, as `parse_json`) is enforced BEFORE allocation. Malformed / truncated / bad-version / over-budget input is an `err(...)`, never a crash. The bytes come straight from `read_bytes`: `parse_native(unwrap(read_bytes(p)))`. |
| `to_json(v[, opts])` | 1-2 | The deterministic encode half of `parse_json`, RESULT-based like it: `ok(json_string)` / `err(message)`. Records become objects with SORTED keys, rank-1 arrays flat lists (higher rank nests by shape), strings JSON-escaped with exact Unicode, integers print bare, `ok(x)`/`err(e)` become `{"ok":true,"value":x}` / `{"ok":false,"error":e}`. Returns `err(...)` for a non-data kind (models, tokenizers, generation state, partials, references, device tensors) or a NON-FINITE number (`NaN`/`±Inf` have no JSON form) -- never a hard error and never invalid JSON. Scalars, rank-1 arrays, strings, string lists, and records of those round-trip through `parse_json` (both sides Result-based: `parse_json(unwrap(to_json(v)))`). With `{tagged: 1}`, a rank-`>=2` array and a Result are emitted as reserved `$mlpl` envelopes (`{shape,data}` / `{variant,...}`) so ANY data value round-trips losslessly -- `parse_json` reconstructs `$mlpl` envelopes unconditionally. |
| `to_toml(record)` | 1 | Deterministic TOML encoder for config-style data, RESULT-based: `ok(toml_text)` / `err(message)`. The root MUST be a record (a TOML document is a table). Fields emit in SORTED order: scalar / string / rank-1-array / string-list fields as `key = value` first, then nested records -- and any `ok(x)`/`err(e)` Result, encoded as a `{ok, value|error}` sub-table so it round-trips with `parse_toml(..., {results: 1})` -- as `[section]` / `[section.sub]` tables. Keys must be bare (`A-Za-z0-9_-`). Returns `err(...)` for a non-record root (a TOML document is a table), a non-finite number, a rank-`>=2` array, or a value with no TOML form (models, tokenizers, ...). Supported value forms: integer, float, basic string, and homogeneous arrays of numbers or strings. NOT supported (an err, or absent on decode): inline tables, arrays of tables, literal/multiline strings, datetimes, and dotted-key assignments. |
| `parse_toml(text[, opts])` | 1-2 | Decode the TOML config subset into a record, RESULT-based: `ok(record)` / `err(message with line)`. Line-oriented: `#` comments and blank lines are skipped, `[table]` / dotted `[table.sub]` headers nest records, `key = value` assigns into the current table. Values reuse the JSON value parser -- integer, float, `true`/`false` (to 1/0), basic string, and homogeneous arrays of numbers or strings. A trailing `# comment` after a value is allowed. Round-trips with `to_toml` for the supported forms: `parse_toml(unwrap(to_toml(record)))`. Accepts the same optional `opts` record as `parse_json` (`max_depth`, `max_bytes`). |
| `run_script(path, opts)` | 1-2 | Execute a script file in a FRESH environment -- definitions, `@test` metadata, and bindings cannot leak between files; `include` and file-accurate spans behave exactly as in normal script runs. Options: `{source_dir, data_dir, capture: 1}` (paths sandbox-resolved). Returns `ok({status, value, error, events_kind, events})`: `status` is `"ok"`, `"err"` (the script's final value was an Err), `"error"` (hard eval error), or `"exit"` with the code in `value` -- the child's `exit(n)` is INTERCEPTED as data instead of terminating the process. `capture: 1` buffers the child's typed test events into `events` (one JSON line each). Only unreadable/unloadable sources are `err(...)`. |
| `global_set(name, v)` | 2 | The EXPLICIT global-state escape hatch: bind `name` to `v` at the workspace level from anywhere -- inside a function frame the write survives the frame restore and propagates to the top level. Ordinary assignment inside a function stays frame-local (binding hygiene is the default); `global_set` is the one spelled-out exception, which is what makes a stateful test-reporter sink (counters across `emit_test_event` calls) expressible. Any value kind; returns the value; malformed names error. |
| `test_event_sink(f)` | 1 | Register ONE `:u:` callback to receive every event `emit_test_event` accepts (builtin references rejected -- sinks are user code). Returns `ok(1)`. |
| `emit_test_event(e)` | 1 | Validate a test-event record against schema version 1 -- `version` scalar 1, `kind` one of `suite_start`/`test_start`/`case_start`/`assertion_failure`/`output`/`test_end`/`case_end`/`teardown_failure`/`suite_end`, `suite` and `name` strings, `status` in `passed`/`failed`/`skipped`/`expected_failure` for `test_end`/`case_end` -- then deliver it to the registered sink and, when a host channel is active, append it as one JSON line (the `--test-events <path>` file in script mode; the eval response's `test_events` array in connect mode). Unknown ADDITIVE fields pass through. A sink failure becomes emit's `err`; with no sink, emit validates only and returns `ok(1)`. |
| `equal(a, b)` | 2 | Total STRUCTURAL equality over any two values: numbers (IEEE, except NaN equals NaN), strings, arrays (shape + axis labels + elements), records (recursing), models, tokenizers, `ok`/`err` results. Mismatched kinds return 0 -- never a hard error -- so assertions stay honest. Returns scalar 1/0. |
| `repr(v)` | 1 | Deterministic, BOUNDED rendering of any value for expected-vs-actual diagnostics: `array[2, 3] [0, 1, ...]` with labels, quoted escaped strings, `{field: ...}` records, `ok(...)`/`err(...)`. Truncates large values with an explicit marker; not a serialization format. |
| `type_of(v)` | 1 | Stable kind string of any value: `array`, `string`, `record`, `result`, `string-list`, `model`, `tokenizer`, `gen-state`, `partial`, `builtin-ref`, `user-fn-ref`, `device-tensor`. Total (never errors), so a program can branch on a root value's kind before calling kind-specific accessors (`has_field`/`record_get` on records, `to_json` on data). |
| `record_keys(record)` | 1 | The record's keys as a string-list, in DETERMINISTIC sorted order (records are sorted-map-backed). | `compress(mask, a[, axis])` | 2-3 | Keep the slices of `a` along `axis` (default 0) where rank-1 `mask` is nonzero (APL compress). `compress(gt(scores, t), C)` keeps verified candidates; works on any rank. |
| `pareto_plot(P, dirs)` | 2 | Render the frontier: every metric pair as a dot (frontier members highlighted), plus the staircase line through the frontier. Computes the mask with `pareto_front` internally, so plot and mask always agree. |
| `pareto_front(P, dirs)` | 2 | The `[n]` 0/1 mask of non-dominated rows of the `[n, k]` metric matrix `P`; `dirs` is `[k]` with `1` = maximize the column, `-1` = minimize. `compress(pareto_front(P, dirs), P)` keeps the frontier; `scatter_labeled(P, pareto_front(P, dirs))` highlights it. |
| `kg_neighbors(edges, node[, rel])` | 2-3 | One-hop destination ids from `node` in an `[E, 3]` `(src, rel, dst)` edge array, sorted and deduplicated; the optional third argument restricts to one relation. |
| `kg_verify(edges, paths)` | 2 | Row-batched path checker: for `[n, L]` id sequences, `out[i]` is 1 when every consecutive pair in row i is an edge (any relation). Rank-1 input is one path. The answer oracle for multi-hop tasks. |
| `kg_paths(edges, hops, n, seed)` | 4 | `[n, hops+1]` valid paths sampled by seeded random walk (uniform start edge, uniform outgoing edge; dead ends restart). Every sampled row passes `kg_verify`. The multi-hop task generator. |
| `kg_split(edges, frac, seed)` | 3 | Entity-disjoint `{seen, unseen}` record: entities are shuffled by seed, the first `frac` become the seen set; an edge is `seen` only if BOTH endpoints are seen entities, so unseen paths must visit entities the seen side never contains. |
| `rand_ints(n, lo, hi, seed)` | 4 | `[n]` uniform integers in `[lo, hi)`, deterministic per seed (explicit PRNG state, same bits everywhere). The integer source for synthetic-data generators; pairs with `randn` (Gaussian floats). |
| `clock_ms()` | 0 | A high-resolution MONOTONIC clock: milliseconds elapsed since a process-start epoch, as a scalar -- only DIFFERENCES are meaningful (`t0 = clock_ms(); ...; dt = clock_ms() - t0`). For benchmarking (inserts/sec, latency). A native + connect-mode builtin (not available in the pure browser playground), like `load`. |
| `band(a, b)` | 2 | Bitwise AND over non-negative integers held as exact `f64` (element-wise, scalar broadcast). Domain is `0..2^53`; negatives / non-integers / out-of-range error loudly. |
| `bor(a, b)` | 2 | Bitwise OR. |
| `bxor(a, b)` | 2 | Bitwise XOR. Hamming distance between two codes is `popcount(bxor(a, b))`. |
| `bnot(x, width)` | 2 | Bitwise complement within `width` bits (`~x & mask(width)`), `width` in `1..=53`. |
| `popcount(x)` | 1 | Count of set bits in each element. |
| `shl(x, k, width)` | 3 | Fixed-width left shift: `(x << k)` masked to `width` bits (so a `u8` shift stays a `u8`; avoids `f64` exactness loss). |
| `shr(x, k)` | 2 | Logical right shift by `k` bits. |
| `bmask(x, width)` | 2 | Keep the low `width` bits -- explicit truncation / width conversion. |
| `bits(x, width)` | 2 | Expand a scalar integer to a `[width]` 0/1 vector, LSB-first (index `i` = bit `i`). |
| `from_bits(v)` | 1 | Pack a rank-1 0/1 vector back to an integer scalar (the inverse of `bits`). |
| `dedupe_rows(X)` | 1 | Unique rows of a rank-2 `[n, L]` array (first occurrence kept, original order) as a `{rows, index}` record: `d.rows` for direct use, `gather_rows(Y, d.index)` to carry companion arrays along. |
| `running_sum(v)` | 1 | Running sum along a rank-1 vector: `out[i]` is the sum of `v[0..=i]` (prefix sums, CDFs, cumulative totals). The additive sibling of `running_product`. | `disp(a)` | 1 | Returns an ASCII box diagram (a `Value::Str`) that makes the rank, shape, and depth of `a` visible: rank <= 2 as a framed grid, rank 3 as a row of boxed matrices, rank 4 as an outer grid of boxed matrices (APL2's DISPLAY of blocks enclosed on the trailing two axes, from a flat array), rank >= 5 as a labeled stack of leading-axis slices, plus a `rank R  shape [..]  depth D` footer. | `emit_frame(name, step, x)` | 3 | Stream tensor `x` as a live frame through the connect-mode metric sink (the whole-tensor analog of `_metric` scalars); a no-op when not connected. Returns `x`. |

| `get_value(r)` | 1 | The Ok side of a Result as a 0-or-1 element vector: `[v]` when `r` is `Ok(v)` (scalar payloads), `[]` when Err. `tally` of it is `is_some`; APL2 zilde-Option flavor (see docs/error-handling.md). |
| `linspace(start, stop, n)` | 3 | `n` evenly-spaced values from `start` to `stop` inclusive, as a rank-1 vector. |
| `range(n)` | 1 | Integers 0, 1, ..., n-1 as a vector (preferred name) `iota(n)` is a DEPRECATED alias (APL heritage): it still evaluates but is absent from docs and examples; prefer `range`. |
| `rank(a)` | 1 | Number of dimensions (scalar) |
| `reduce(:op, a)` | 2 | Higher-order reduction: `:op` is one of `:add`/`:+`, `:mul`/`:*`, `:min`, `:max`, `:and`, `:or`. Examples: `reduce(:max, v)`, `reduce(:and, mask)`. The first argument is a `BuiltinRef` (`:foo` syntax); user variables can hold one too: `f = :max; reduce(f, v)`. |

| `reduce(:op, a, axis)` | 3 | Same, restricted to a single axis. |
| `reduce_add(a[, axis])` | 1-2 | Sum all elements (or along axis). Equivalent to `reduce(:add, a[, axis])`; kept as a direct shorthand. |
| `reduce_mul(a[, axis])` | 1-2 | Product. Equivalent to `reduce(:mul, a[, axis])`. |
| `apply_engram(e, h, ids)` | 3 | Engram forward pass: hash the ids, gather the addressed memory rows, project, concat-gate against `h`, and add to the residual stream. # sw-MLPL Data Structures and Algorithms

General-purpose data-structure and algorithm demonstrations written as
standalone `.mlpl` scripts for the
[sw-MLPL](https://sw-ml-study.github.io/sw-mlpl/) interpreter.

This repository has two jobs:

1. Show that an array language designed around modern ML can also explain
   dynamically sized structures and ordinary programming clearly, with few
   explicit loops and preferably none.
2. Act as a forcing function: when a normal algorithm is awkward or
   impossible, record the missing language capability precisely and turn it
   into an executable acceptance case for sw-MLPL.

The demonstrations deliberately favor pure transformations, function
composition, delegation, and whole-array operations. An explicit loop is a
baseline or a last resort, not the intended destination. A sorting demo should
still expose the algorithm rather than merely call `grade_up`; the challenge is
to express its phases through reusable array combinators.

## Status

### Verified tools

Verified baseline: `mlpl-repl 0.20.0`, local build commit `d373584c`
(2026-08-11), with mlplunit `0.1.0` at commit `a06191f`. The adjacent
source checkout contained unrelated in-progress changes when rebuilt; the MLPB
v2 codec itself shipped in committed revision `00945f7d`.

### Executable corpus

The repository now contains 96 working mini-apps and 88 conformance-test
files, reporting 192 native tests and parameter cases, as well as the longer
implementation plan.

### Core design and roadmap

- [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) covers the taxonomy, capability analysis, proposed file
  tree, feature gaps, and delivery sequence.
=== catalog README ===
# Demo catalog

The catalogs are machine-readable inventories consumed by the runners:

- `demos.tsv` contains only problem-solving mini-apps that show a meaningful
  result.
- `tests.tsv` contains `test_*.mlpl` assertion/pass-fail conformance scripts
  executed through mlplunit in isolated interpreter processes.

Both use the same tab-separated fields so the harness needs no package manager
or third-party parser.

Required columns:

| Column | Contract |
|---|---|
| `id` | Stable lowercase identifier using letters, digits, `_`, or `-` |
| `path` | Repository-relative `.mlpl` path under the catalog's matching `demos/` or `tests/` tree |
| `data_structure` | Primary structure demonstrated |
| `algorithm` | Operation or algorithm demonstrated |
| `dynamic_size` | `yes` or `no` |
| `explicit_loops` | Non-negative integer in the current script |
| `target_loops` | Non-negative integer after planned language features |
| `required_features` | Comma-separated feature IDs, or `current` |
| `status` | `runnable`, `constrained`, or `gated` |

`runnable` and `constrained` entries must name an existing script. A `gated`
entry may name its planned location before the script exists. The catalog
validator rejects duplicate IDs and paths, cross-kind paths, malformed values,
missing files, and a target loop count larger than the current count.
=== demos tree ===

patterns
=== scripts/run-all ===
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

repo_root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
catalog=${CATALOG:-"$repo_root/catalog/demos.tsv"}
mlpl=${MLPL:-"$repo_root/../sw-mlpl/target/release/mlpl-repl"}

"$repo_root/scripts/validate-catalog" "$catalog"
"$repo_root/scripts/check-docstrings"

if [ ! -x "$mlpl" ]; then
  echo "mlpl-repl is not executable: $mlpl" >&2
  echo "set MLPL=/absolute/path/to/mlpl-repl" >&2
  exit 1
fi

failures=0
ran=0
tab=$(printf '\t')
while IFS="$tab" read -r id path data_structure algorithm dynamic_size explicit_loops target_loops required_features status; do
  [ "$id" = "id" ] && continue
  [ -z "$id" ] && continue
  [ "$status" = "gated" ] && continue
  ran=$((ran + 1))
  echo "RUN $id ($data_structure: $algorithm)"
  if ! "$mlpl" --source-dir "$repo_root" "$repo_root/$path"; then
    echo "FAIL $id" >&2
    failures=$((failures + 1))
  else
    echo "PASS $id"
  fi
done < "$catalog"

echo "Ran $ran demo(s); $failures failure(s)."
[ "$failures" -eq 0 ]

```text
@test
def u:addition_works() { u:assert_eq(2 + 2, 4, "adds") }

@test {name: "beta case", tags: ["fast"], timeout_ms: 500}
@formula "H(p) = -sum(p * log(p))"
def u:entropy(p) { 0 - sum(p * log(p)) }
```

`@word [record-literal | string-literal]` lines annotate the
NEXT `def u:` statement; several annotations stack onto one
definition. An annotation followed by anything other than a
`def` is a parse error, as is a bare `@` with no word.

`@` is a general namespace: any word is legal, and every
annotation is preserved as data readable via
`annotations(name)` -- so documentation or formula metadata
costs no language support. Exactly one word is INTERPRETED:
`@test` registers the definition in the test registry at the
moment the `def` evaluates (so include splice order is
registration order). Its optional record payload is validated
-- unknown or mistyped fields are an error. Recognized fields,
all optional: `name` (stable test name; default the function
name without `u:`), `tags` (string list), `skip` (string
reason; presence means skip), `expected_failure` (scalar 1
inverts pass/fail), `timeout_ms` (scalar; recorded for the
runner, not enforced by the evaluator). Duplicate stable names
across different functions are an error naming both
definitions; re-defining a test function replaces its entry in
place. Discovery is side-effect-free: `tests()` lists stable
names in registration order and `test_info(name)` returns one
registry row whose `fn` field is the `:u:` reference, so a
runner invokes it with `call(test_info(n).fn)`.

## Experiment Block

```
experiment "name" { body }
```

A scoped form that records every scalar assigned to a name ending
in `_metric` during the body, along with the shapes of any `param`
bindings. The record lands in the REPL's in-memory experiment log
(web REPL) and also on disk under `--exp-dir/<name>/<timestamp>/run.json`
when the terminal REPL is invoked with `--exp-dir`.

```
experiment "baseline" {
  train 50 { adam(loss, model, 0.01, 0.9, 0.999, 0.00000001); loss };
  loss_metric = loss
}
compare("baseline", "variant")
:experiments
```

### Streaming metrics (connect mode)

When a program runs on a connected `mlpl-serve` peer, every `train`
iteration also streams metrics to the client as SSE `metric` frames,
driving the web playground's live loss panel and LOSS sparkline row:

- every scalar bound to a `*_metric` name inside the block streams
  per step under that name (a `val`-prefixed name, e.g.
  `val_loss_metric`, charts as the validation series);
- when the block binds NO `*_metric` name, the block's own per-step
  loss (its final expression, the same scalar that fills
  `last_losses`) streams as the implicit `loss` metric -- so a plain
  `train N { ... }` shows a live loss curve with no extra code and no
  recompute.

## Labeled Axes

An assignment may carry axis labels as metadata so label mismatches
in downstream ops surface with a `ShapeMismatch` error that names
both labeled shapes. Labels propagate through elementwise ops,
matmul (contraction axis validated), reductions (the reduced axis's
label drops), and `map()`.

```
M : [batch, feat] = reshape(range(6), [2, 3])
labels(M)                         # "batch,feat"
reduce_add(M, "feat")             # reduce by axis name
labels(transpose(M))              # swaps labels alongside dims
```

See `label(x, [...])`, `relabel(x, [...])`, and
`reshape_labeled(x, dims, labels)` in the built-ins table.

## Parameters and Autograd

```
W = param[2, 3]        # trainable leaf; tape-tracked
T = tensor[2, 3]       # non-trainable tape tensor
grad(loss_expr, W)     # gradient of a scalar wrt a param
```

`param[shape]` declares a zero-initialized trainable leaf
(typically immediately overwritten with `randn(seed, shape) * scale`).
`tensor[shape]` declares an ordinary tape-tracked tensor. `grad`
lifts an array expression onto the reverse-mode tape and returns
the gradient with the same shape as the `wrt` operand.

## Comments

```
# this is a comment
x = 42  # inline comment
```

`#` starts a line comment that runs to end of line.

## Statement Separation

```
x = 1; y = 2        # semicolon separates
x = 1
y = 2                # newline separates
```

Newlines and semicolons are both statement separators.

## Table Ordering Policy

Lookup tables and listings in this reference (and in `:builtins` /
`:vars` / `:fns` output) sort ALPHABETICALLY within their group --
groups exist only where they aid discovery. Time-ordered logs
(`:experiments`, CHANGES) stay chronological; short narrative
tables (e.g. the three name forms) keep their teaching order.

## Built-in Functions

# Feasibility spike: loop-free algebraic law checking over a Cayley table.

T = [[0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 2], [0, 2, 2]]      # rock-paper-scissors "winner"
n = tally(T)

print("cayley table")
print(disp(T))

# Closure: every entry is a valid element index.
closed = reduce(:and, flatten(mul(ge(T, 0), lt(T, n))))
print("closed:", closed)

# Commutativity: T equals its transpose.
commutative = equal(T, transpose(T))
print("commutative:", commutative)

# Associativity, no explicit loops:
#   L[a,b,c] = T[T[a,b], c]
#   R[a,b,c] = T[a, T[b,c]]
L = reshape(gather_rows(T, flatten(T)), [n, n, n])
M = reshape(gather_rows(transpose(T), flatten(T)), [n, n, n])   # M[b,c,a]
R = transpose_axes(M, [2, 0, 1])
agree = eq(L, R)
associative = reduce(:and, flatten(agree))
print("associative:", associative)

# First counterexample triple, still loop-free.
flat = flatten(agree)
first_bad = take(grade_up(flat), 0, 0)
a = floor(first_bad / (n * n))
b = floor(mod(first_bad, n * n) / n)
c = mod(first_bad, n)
print("counterexample a,b,c:", a, b, c)

# Identity: a row that reproduces the header and a column that does too.
hdr = range(n)
row_ok = reduce(:and, eq(T, hdr), 1)
col_ok = reduce(:and, eq(transpose(T), hdr), 1)
identity_mask = mul(row_ok, col_ok)
print("identity mask:", identity_mask)

svg_text = svg(T, "heatmap")
print("svg bytes:", size(tokenize_bytes(svg_text)))
ok("spike complete")

# Feasibility spike: loop-free algebraic law checking over a Cayley table.

T = [[0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 2], [0, 2, 2]]      # rock-paper-scissors "winner"
n = tally(T)

print("cayley table")
print(disp(T))

# Closure: every entry is a valid element index.  No ge/le builtins, so
# "not less than 0" is spelled 1 - lt(...).
closed = reduce(:and, flatten((1 - lt(T, 0)) * lt(T, n)))
print("closed:", closed)

# Commutativity: T equals its transpose.
commutative = equal(T, transpose(T))
print("commutative:", commutative)

# Associativity, no explicit loops:
#   L[a,b,c] = T[T[a,b], c]
#   R[a,b,c] = T[a, T[b,c]]
L = reshape(gather_rows(T, flatten(T)), [n, n, n])
M = reshape(gather_rows(transpose(T), flatten(T)), [n, n, n])   # M[b,c,a]
R = transpose_axes(M, [2, 0, 1])
agree = eq(L, R)
associative = reduce(:and, flatten(agree))
print("associative:", associative)

# First counterexample triple, still loop-free.
flat = flatten(agree)
first_bad = take(grade_up(flat), 0, 0)
a = floor(first_bad / (n * n))
b = floor(mod(first_bad, n * n) / n)
c = mod(first_bad, n)
print("first disagreeing (a, b, c):", a, b, c)
print("  (a*b)*c =", take(take(take(L, 0, a), 0, b), 0, c))
print("  a*(b*c) =", take(take(take(R, 0, a), 0, b), 0, c))

# Identity: a row that reproduces the header and a column that does too.
hdr = range(n)
row_ok = reduce(:and, eq(T, hdr), 1)
col_ok = reduce(:and, eq(transpose(T), hdr), 1)
identity_mask = row_ok * col_ok
print("identity mask:", identity_mask)

# table() builds the same Cayley table from a function.
def u:add3(x, y) { mod(x + y, 3) }
C = table(:u:add3, hdr, hdr)
print("cyclic group Z3 via table():")
print(disp(C))

svg_text = svg(T, "heatmap")
print("svg type:", type_of(svg_text))
w = write_text("spike-rps.svg", svg_text)
print("wrote svg:", is_ok(w))
j = to_json({elements: ["rock", "paper", "scissors"], table: T}, {tagged: 1})
print("json ok:", is_ok(j))
print(unwrap(j))
ok("spike complete")

Manage shared agent briefing — the global instructions clearinghouse

Renders embedded `agent-instructions/` fragments into a markered block in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md (or the targets configured in `.agentrail/instruction-profile.toml`), preserving everything outside the markers. The lock file `.agentrail/instruction-lock.toml` records the profile name, content hash, and timestamp of the last apply.

The canonical source lives in `agent-instructions/` at the workspace root and is bundled into the binary at compile time. To change the shared rules: edit the fragments, commit, rebuild (e.g. `sw-install`), and re-run `agentrail instructions apply` in each project.

PER-REPO CONFIG (.agentrail/instruction-profile.toml, all optional):

profile     = "default"                       # name of an embedded profile; #   see `instructions list` targets     = ["CLAUDE.md", "AGENTS.md"]      # files that receive the #   briefing block; defaults #   to whichever of those two #   already exist auto_apply  = false                           # if true, `agentrail next` #   rewrites stale blocks #   in-place + tells the agent #   to re-read CLAUDE.md exclude     = ["global/push-discipline.md"]   # fragment paths to drop from #   the resolved profile; #   unknown entries are #   silently ignored so #   per-repo configs survive #   maintainer-side renames

The lock-file content_hash, the freshness check, and the diff command all reflect the post-exclude render, so a repo that intentionally drops a fragment stays "up to date" without churn.

`instruction-profile.toml` is user config (like `.gitconfig`). Hand-edit it freely, or use `agentrail instructions profile *` to mutate via commands — both are valid. The agentrail-managed files in `.agentrail/` are `saga.toml` / `step.toml` / session JSONLs / trajectory JSONs (don't hand-edit those).

Usage: agentrail instructions <COMMAND>

  help     Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

  set -- "$@" "$repo_root/$path"
done < "$catalog"

# Agent Instructions

This repository uses the AgentRail saga/step process. The generated shared
briefing above is mandatory and is sourced from the same AgentRail instruction
profile used by the adjacent `../sw-mlpl` repository. This repository has no
`CLAUDE.md`; do not infer that one is required or create a duplicate
instruction file merely for symmetry with a sibling repository.

## What this repository is

Executable, **visual** demonstrations of abstract algebra — magmas,
semigroups, monoids, groups, and the structure-preserving maps between them —
written as standalone `.mlpl` scripts for the sw-MLPL interpreter.

Two jobs, in this order:

1. **Teach the algebra visually.** A finite binary operation is an `n x n`
   Cayley table, which is an array, which sw-MLPL renders. Every lesson must
   produce something a learner can *look at* — an ASCII `disp()` grid, an SVG
   table with highlighted rows/columns, or a page in `viewer/`. A lesson that
   only prints `associative: 0` has failed its brief.
2. **Act as a forcing function.** When a law check, an enumeration, or a
   rendering is awkward or impossible in ordinary `.mlpl`, record the missing
   capability precisely in `docs/upstream-asks.md` as an executable acceptance
   case. Do not work around friction silently.

## Scope boundary — read before adding a lesson

This repository covers **abstract algebra only**. Category theory
(categories, functors, natural transformations, monads, adjunctions) is
deferred to the adjacent `../demo-category-theory` repository and is worked by
a different agent.

`docs/scope-boundary.md` is the contract. Consult it before starting work that
mentions functors, morphisms, or composition laws. The one shared surface is
the **homomorphism** — structure-preserving maps between algebraic structures
live here; the categorical reading of them lives there.

Do not edit `../demo-category-theory`, `../sw-mlpl`, or any other sibling
repository from a session working in this one.

## Project rules adapted from sw-MLPL

- Follow `agentrail next`, `agentrail begin`, work, test, commit,
  `agentrail complete`, then stop. Never edit `.agentrail/` by hand.
- Use TDD for executable behavior. Add a failing fixture or assertion before
  or with the implementation that satisfies it.
- Keep functions small and single-purpose. Prefer pure free functions,
  top-down delegation, composition, and define-once/invoke-many helpers.
- Separate decisions from effects: `.mlpl` functions compute values; the thin
  runner performs process and filesystem effects.
- Every commit must leave the scoped demo suite green.
- Update the catalog and user-facing documentation in the same step as a demo.
- Do not install or overwrite the user's stable sw-MLPL binaries. Run the
  explicitly configured binary from `$MLPL` or the documented adjacent build.
- Do not modify `../sw-mlpl`; language changes belong to a separately
  authorized upstream task. Record the ask in `docs/upstream-asks.md` instead.
- Do not continue making changes after `agentrail complete`; additional work
  belongs to the next step.

## Task runner policy

- Use the repository `justfile` and `just` recipes as the preferred human and
  agent entry points for routine tasks.
- Do not introduce a `Makefile` or invoke `make` unless the user explicitly
  requests Make compatibility for a concrete external integration.
- Keep recipes thin: delegate to the existing scripts rather than copying
  catalog, mlplunit, binary-selection, or validation logic into the `justfile`.
- Direct script commands remain supported for minimal environments and for
  debugging the delegated layer.

## Demo quality rules

- Standalone `.mlpl`, deterministic, and self-checking.
- End with `ok(...)` on success and `err(...)` on failed invariants.
- Exercise empty, singleton, boundary, duplicate, and invalid cases where
  applicable.
- Prefer whole-array operations, pure functions, and delegation. Explain every
  remaining explicit loop and the future combinator that could remove it.
- Document logical complexity and the explicit-loop count in the header
  comment.
- Treat strings as static messages and labels wherever possible; the byte-array
  concatenation idiom (`lib/text.mlpl`) is permitted only where a lesson must
  emit its own SVG or HTML.

## Visual output rules

- Every lesson writes its artifacts under `out/` (gitignored). No lesson
  writes anywhere else.
- A lesson's textual assertions must pass with `out/` deleted; rendering is an
  additional effect, never the thing under test.
- Terminal-visible output comes first (`disp()` grids), then file artifacts
  (SVG), then the interactive page (`viewer/`).
- `viewer/` pages are dependency-free, single-file HTML. No CDN, no build step.
- Where a viewer re-implements a law check in JavaScript for interactivity, the
  MLPL result is authoritative: `tests/test_viewer_conformance.mlpl` pins the
  fixture the page is checked against.

## Terminology discipline

A stated goal of this repository is that words that collide across branches of
mathematics are disambiguated, not glossed over. Every lesson README carries a
`Meaning here / Also called / Not to be confused with` block. See
`docs/terminology.md`.

## Scope and references

- Implementation plan and lesson sequence: `docs/plan.md`
- Repository boundary with demo-category-theory: `docs/scope-boundary.md`
- Language friction found while building lessons: `docs/upstream-asks.md`
- Word-collision glossary: `docs/terminology.md`
- Source brief: `docs/research.txt`

42	
43	### 5. COMPLETE — `agentrail complete`
44	```
45	agentrail complete --summary "what you accomplished" \
46	  --reward 1 \
47	  --actions "tools and approach used"
48	```
49	On failure: `--reward -1 --failure-mode "what went wrong"`.
50	On final step: add `--done`.
51	
52	### 6. STOP
53	After `complete`, do NOT make further code changes. Anything after
54	`complete` is untracked and invisible to the next session. If you see more
55	work to do, it belongs in the NEXT step, not this one.
56	
57	## Agentrail metadata discipline
58	
59	When using agentrail, changes to `.agentrail/` files are first-class project
60	changes — the same as application source code. They must be committed, and
61	should be pushed before you hand off.
62	
63	Before running `agentrail complete`:
64	
65	1. `git status` — confirm `.agentrail/` files are tracked, not just present.
66	   Untracked files in `.agentrail/` mean the next session will not see them.
67	2. Stage and commit source changes and `.agentrail/` metadata together. The
68	   commit recorded into the step's `commits` field comes from `HEAD` at the
69	   moment of `agentrail complete`, so the commit must happen *first*.
70	3. Run `agentrail complete` after the commit lands.
71	4. Push the branch (or note the unpushed branch state in your handoff).
72	
73	This is the most common agentrail failure mode: agents do the work, commit
74	the source, and forget the `.agentrail/` files. The result is a saga whose
75	recorded history disagrees with git history, which `agentrail audit` will
76	flag — but only after the damage is done.
77	
78	### What's hand-editable in `.agentrail/`
79	
80	Three categories of files live here, and the rules differ:
81	
82	- **Append-only saga state** — `saga.toml`, `step.toml`, `plan.md`, session
83	  JSONLs under `sessions/`, trajectory JSONs under `trajectories/`, and
84	  anything under `.agentrail-archive/`. **Never hand-edit or delete these.**
85	  They are written by agentrail commands and represent the durable saga
86	  record; hand-editing desyncs the saga from git history and from prior
87	  session memory. A direct `rm` on untracked files is unrecoverable.
88	- **Regenerated state** — `instruction-lock.toml`. Don't hand-edit; it is
89	  rewritten on every `agentrail instructions apply`, so any local changes
90	  are overwritten silently.
91	- **User config** — `instruction-profile.toml`. This is normal user-edited
92	  config, like `.gitconfig` or a `package.json`. Hand-edit it freely, or
93	  use `agentrail instructions profile *` subcommands to mutate via
94	  commands (which validate field values and surface typos).
95	
96	## Branch handoff after `agentrail complete`
97	
98	Once a feature branch is committed and `agentrail complete` has run,
99	signal that it is ready for review/merge by renaming it from
100	`feat/<slug>` to `pr/<slug>`:
101	
102	```bash
103	git branch -m feat/<slug> pr/<slug>
104	```
105	
106	The rename is a useful convention regardless of how this project
107	handles handoff:
108	
109	- It distinguishes "in-progress work" from "awaiting review" in the
110	  output of `git branch`.
111	- Project-specific tooling (CI, release-engineer scans, automated PR
112	  creation) can key off the `pr/*` prefix.
113	- It keeps the branch name stable across the review cycle even if the
114	  feature slug evolves.
115	
116	What happens after the rename depends on what push capability you
117	have. See `push-discipline.md` for how to detect capability before
118	trying.
119	
120	- **You can push and use GitHub PRs.** Push the renamed branch and
121	  open the PR:
122	  ```bash
123	  git push -u origin pr/<slug>
124	  gh pr create
125	  ```
126	  (Or push and open the PR via the web UI.)
127	- **You cloned via HTTPS without push access to the upstream remote.**
128	  Typical when contributing to an open-source project you don't own:
129	  push the renamed branch to your fork instead, then open the PR
130	  pointing at upstream. `git remote -v` shows your remotes; add a
131	  fork remote with `git remote add fork <url>` if needed.
132	- **Your project has a project-specific handoff flow** (release
133	  engineer scanning for `pr/*` branches, automated PR creation, CI
134	  hooks). The rename IS the handoff signal. Look for site-specific
135	  guidance in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers — if
136	  present, follow that instead.
137	
138	After the rename, do not continue committing to `pr/<slug>` — those
139	commits will not be in the PR. Start further work on a fresh branch
140	off the (eventually merged and pulled) base.
141	
142	## Push discipline
143	
144	When you push (typically after `branch-handoff` has renamed `feat/X`
145	to `pr/X` and you're publishing the PR branch), do it safely.
146	
147	### Verify push capability before assuming it works
148	
149	- `git remote get-url origin` — `git@…` (SSH) or `https://…` plus a
150	  configured credential helper is push-capable. A bare `https://…`
151	  with no helper usually is not (read-only mirror or fresh clone).
152	- `gh auth status` — if the project uses GitHub PRs and `gh` is not
153	  authenticated, `gh pr create` will fail.
154	- `git push --dry-run` — surfaces auth or branch-protection problems
155	  without changing remote state.
156	
157	### If you cannot push (or push fails)
158	
159	- Note the unpushed branch state explicitly in your `agentrail
160	  complete --summary` so the next session knows the work is local.
161	- Do NOT silently leave commits stranded on a local branch — the next
162	  agent will look at the remote and assume your work was lost.
163	- Do NOT retry the same `git push` in a loop. If the failure is a
164	  permission issue (no SSH key, no `gh` auth, sandboxed user), retries
165	  will not fix it. Surface the failure to the user.
166	- If this project has a project-specific handoff flow (release
167	  engineer scans for `pr/*` branches, queue files, CI hooks
168	  documented in CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md outside the briefing markers),
169	  follow that instead of pushing — the branch rename from
170	  `branch-handoff.md` may already be sufficient.
171	
172	### If the remote rejects a push
173	
174	- For non-fast-forward errors on a personal branch, prefer
175	  `git pull --rebase` over `--force` unless the user has explicitly
176	  authorized force-push.

# Validate a catalog TSV: header contract, unique ids/paths, well-formed
# values, existing files for non-gated rows, and target_loops <= explicit_loops.
set -eu

catalog=${1:?usage: validate-catalog <catalog.tsv>}

case "$catalog" in
  /*) catalog_path=$catalog ;;
  *) catalog_path="$repo_root/$catalog" ;;

  *) tree=demos ;;

NR == 1 {
  expected = "id\tpath\tlesson\tconcept\texplicit_loops\ttarget_loops\tvisual\trequired_features\tstatus"
  if ($0 != expected) { printf "%s: bad header\n  want: %s\n  got:  %s\n", name, expected, $0 > "/dev/stderr"; bad = 1 }
  next
}
/^[[:space:]]*$/ { next }
{
  if (NF != 9) { printf "%s:%d: expected 9 fields, got %d\n", name, NR, NF > "/dev/stderr"; bad = 1; next }

  if (id !~ /^[a-z0-9_-]+$/) { printf "%s:%d: bad id %s\n", name, NR, id > "/dev/stderr"; bad = 1 }
  if (id in seen_id) { printf "%s:%d: duplicate id %s\n", name, NR, id > "/dev/stderr"; bad = 1 }

  if (target !~ /^[0-9]+$/) { printf "%s:%d: target_loops must be an integer\n", name, NR > "/dev/stderr"; bad = 1 }

' "$catalog_path"

repo_root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd)
failures=0

  esac

[ "$failures" -eq 0 ] || exit 1
echo "docstrings: ok"

# lib/algebra.mlpl -- finite algebraic structures as arrays.
#
# A finite binary operation on n elements IS an n x n Cayley table T, where
# T[a, b] is the index of a * b.  Every law in this repository is therefore an
# array predicate over T, checked without an explicit loop.
#
# Element identity is the index 0 .. n-1 throughout; human names live beside
# the table in a string list, never inside it.
#
# loops: 0

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Construction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# The [n] header vector 0 .. n-1: the element indices, and the row/column
# headings of every Cayley table.
def u:elements(n) { range(n) }

# Element index count for a table.
def u:order(t) { tally(t) }

# The [n, n] matrix whose every row is the header (H[a, b] = b).  sw-MLPL
# broadcasts SCALARS only, so a rank-1 header cannot be compared against a
# rank-2 table directly; this materializes it.  See docs/upstream-asks.md #2.
def u:second(x, y) { y }
def u:header_matrix(n) { table(:u:second, u:elements(n), u:elements(n)) }

# The [n, n] matrix whose every column is the header (K[a, b] = a).
def u:first(x, y) { x }
def u:index_matrix(n) { table(:u:first, u:elements(n), u:elements(n)) }

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The two associativity cubes
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# These are the whole trick.  For a table T of order n:
#
#   left_cube(T)[a, b, c]  = T[T[a, b], c]   -- (a * b) * c
#   right_cube(T)[a, b, c] = T[a, T[b, c]]   -- a * (b * c)
#
# gather_rows(T, flatten(T)) indexes T by every entry of T at once, producing
# the [n*n, n] matrix whose (a*n + b, c) cell is T[T[a, b], c].  Reshaping to
# [n, n, n] is the left cube.  The right cube is the same gather against the
# transpose, which yields axes in (b, c, a) order and is permuted back.
#
# All n^3 triples, no loop.

def u:left_cube(t) {
  n = u:order(t)
  reshape(gather_rows(t, flatten(t)), [n, n, n])
}

def u:right_cube(t) {
  n = u:order(t)
  reshape(gather_rows(transpose(t), flatten(t)), [n, n, n])
}

# The [n, n, n] 0/1 cube: 1 where the two bracketings agree.
def u:assoc_cube(t) {
  eq(u:left_cube(t), transpose_axes(u:right_cube(t), [2, 0, 1]))
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Law predicates -- each returns scalar 1 or 0
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Closure: every entry names a real element.  No ge/le builtins exist, so
# "not below zero" is spelled 1 - lt(...).  See docs/upstream-asks.md #1.
def u:is_closed(t) {
  n = u:order(t)
  reduce(:and, flatten((1 - lt(t, 0)) * lt(t, n) * eq(t, floor(t))))
}

def u:is_associative(t) { reduce(:and, flatten(u:assoc_cube(t))) }

def u:is_commutative(t) { equal(t, transpose(t)) }

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Identity and inverses
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# [n] mask: 1 at each two-sided identity.  Element e is an identity when row e
# reproduces the header AND column e does too.
def u:identity_mask(t) {
  h = u:header_matrix(u:order(t))
  reduce(:and, eq(t, h), 1) * reduce(:and, eq(transpose(t), h), 1)
}

def u:has_identity(t) { reduce(:or, u:identity_mask(t)) }

# The identity element index, or -1 when there is none.  A monoid's identity
# is unique, so argmax over the mask is exact.
def u:identity_of(t) {
  m = u:identity_mask(t)
  argmax(m) * reduce(:or, m) - (1 - reduce(:or, m))
}

# [n, n] mask: 1 where a * b equals the identity, i.e. b is a right inverse of
# a.  Meaningless without an identity, so it is gated to the zero matrix.
def u:inverse_mask(t) {
  e = u:identity_of(t)
  eq(t, e) * u:has_identity(t)
}

# [n] mask: 1 at each element with a two-sided inverse.
def u:invertible_mask(t) {
  right = reduce(:or, u:inverse_mask(t), 1)
  left = reduce(:or, u:inverse_mask(t), 0)
  right * left
}

def u:has_inverses(t) { reduce(:and, u:invertible_mask(t)) }

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Classification -- the ladder is DERIVED, never declared
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Rungs, as a record of 0/1 flags.  A structure is whatever its laws say it is.
def u:classify(t) {
  closed = u:is_closed(t)
  assoc = u:is_associative(t)
  ident = u:has_identity(t)
  inv = u:has_inverses(t)
  comm = u:is_commutative(t)
  {
    closed: closed,
    associative: assoc,
    commutative: comm,
    identity: ident,
    inverses: inv,
    magma: closed,
    semigroup: closed * assoc,
    monoid: closed * assoc * ident,
    group: closed * assoc * ident * inv,
    abelian_group: closed * assoc * ident * inv * comm

# lib/render.mlpl -- turning Cayley tables into things a learner can look at.
#
# sw-MLPL has no string concatenation operator and no number-to-string builtin,
# so both are constructed here from the primitives that do exist:
#
#   concat: decode_bytes(concat(tokenize_bytes(a), tokenize_bytes(b)))
#   number: unwrap(to_json(x))         -- to_json of a scalar IS its digits
#
# Both are recorded as friction in docs/upstream-asks.md (#3, #4).  They are
# confined to this file so that lesson scripts stay readable.
#
# The built-in svg(t, "heatmap") colors a table but draws no headings, no cell
# values, and no highlights, which is most of what teaches (upstream ask #5).
# cayley_svg below emits its own SVG instead.
#
# loops: 0

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# String primitives
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def u:cat(a, b) { decode_bytes(concat(tokenize_bytes(a), tokenize_bytes(b))) }
def u:cat3(a, b, c) { u:cat(a, u:cat(b, c)) }
def u:cat5(a, b, c, d, e) { u:cat(u:cat3(a, b, c), u:cat(d, e)) }
def u:num(x) { unwrap(to_json(x)) }

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# SVG fragments
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def u:svg_open(w, h) {
  u:cat5("<svg xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/2000/svg\" viewBox=\"0 0 ",
    u:num(w), " ", u:num(h),
    "\" font-family=\"ui-monospace,Menlo,monospace\" font-size=\"13\">")
}

def u:svg_rect(x, y, w, h, fill) {
  u:cat5(u:cat5("<rect x=\"", u:num(x), "\" y=\"", u:num(y), "\" width=\""),
    u:num(w), "\" height=\"", u:num(h),
    u:cat3("\" fill=\"", fill, "\"/>"))
}

def u:svg_text(x, y, fill, s) {
  u:cat5(u:cat5("<text x=\"", u:num(x), "\" y=\"", u:num(y), "\" fill=\""),
    fill, "\" text-anchor=\"middle\" dominant-baseline=\"central\">", s, "</text>")
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ASCII: the first visual, and the one that always works
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Print a table as a labelled operation grid with its element names.
def u:show_table(title, names, t) {
  print(title)
  print("  elements:", names)
  print(disp(t))
}

# Print a classification record as a law checklist.
def u:show_laws(t) {
  c = u:classify(t)
  print("  closed      ", u:tick(c.closed))
  print("  associative ", u:tick(c.associative))
  print("  commutative ", u:tick(c.commutative))
  print("  identity    ", u:tick(c.identity))
  print("  inverses    ", u:tick(c.inverses))
  print("  =>", u:structure_name(t))
}

def u:tick(b) { unwrap(list_get(["no", "yes"], b)) }

# Print an associativity failure the way a teaching system should: with the
# witness spelled out, not just a boolean.
def u:show_assoc_counterexample(names, t) {
  x = u:assoc_counterexample(t)
  print("  associativity counterexample:")
  print("    a =", unwrap(list_get(names, x.a)),
        " b =", unwrap(list_get(names, x.b)),
        " c =", unwrap(list_get(names, x.c)))
  print("    (a*b)*c: a*b =", unwrap(list_get(names, x.ab)),
        "-> (a*b)*c =", unwrap(list_get(names, x.left)))
  print("    a*(b*c): b*c =", unwrap(list_get(names, x.bc)),
        "-> a*(b*c) =", unwrap(list_get(names, x.right)))
  x
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# JSON: the transport to viewer/ pages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Everything a viewer page needs about one structure, as a JSON string.
def u:structure_json(name, names, t) {
  c = u:classify(t)
  unwrap(to_json({
    name: name,
    elements: names,
    table: t,
    laws: c,
    structure: u:structure_name(t),
    identity: u:identity_of(t),
    identity_mask: u:identity_mask(t),
    invertible_mask: u:invertible_mask(t),
    assoc_counterexample: u:assoc_counterexample(t),
    comm_counterexample: u:comm_counterexample(t)
  }, {tagged: 1}))
}

content.content:
## Loop Construct

```
repeat N { body }
```

Execute the body N times. N must evaluate to a non-negative integer.
The body can contain multiple statements separated by semicolons or
newlines. Returns the result of the last expression in the final
iteration (or scalar 0 if N is 0).

```
x = 0
repeat 10 { x = x + 1 }
# x is now 10
```

## Training Loop

```
train N { body }
```

Like `repeat`, but additionally binds the iteration index to `step`
inside the body and captures each iteration's final expression value
into a `last_losses` 1-D array in the environment. Use with
`momentum_sgd` / `adam` for training loops:

```
train 100 {
  adam(loss_expr, model, 0.01, 0.9, 0.999, 0.00000001);
  loss_expr
}
loss_curve(last_losses)
```

## For-Row Iteration

```
for ident in expr { body }
```

Iterates `ident` over each rank-(r-1) slice of a rank-r array along
axis 0. The body runs once per slice; each iteration's final value
is collected into a `last_rows` vector in the environment (mirrors
`train`'s `last_losses`). Use for streaming over a dataset when a
full batched representation doesn't fit:

```
for row in reshape(range(6), [3, 2]) { reduce_add(row) }
last_rows   # [1, 5, 9]
```

## Include Declaration

### if / else expression

`if cond { then } else { else }` returns the value of whichever
branch is chosen. The `else` clause is required (no dangling-if).
Both bodies are statement sequences, with the final statement's
value being the branch value -- same convention as `repeat` /
`train` / `for` blocks.

`cond` is truthy when:

- It is a scalar `Number` and not zero (any non-zero value,
  including negatives, NaN, and infinity).
- It is a `Result` and its `ok` field is true (i.e. `Ok(_)`).

Other types (non-scalar arrays, strings, string lists, records,
etc.) raise a runtime error.

```mlpl
flag = 1
x = if flag { 100 } else { 200 }    # x = 100

# Result-as-condition: branches on the Ok / Err discriminant.
name = unwrap_or(env("USER"), "guest")
greeting = if env("USER") { "hello " + name } else { "no user" }

# Nested:
sign = if x { if x > 0 { 1 } else { -1 } } else { 0 }
```

### while / break / continue

`while cond { body }` re-evaluates `body` until `cond` is falsy
(same truthiness rule as `if`) or `break` fires. The expression
evaluates to:

- the `break value` if the loop exited via `break value`
- scalar `0` if the loop exited via bare `break`
- scalar `0` if the loop exited because `cond` went falsy

`continue` skips the rest of the current iteration; the condition
is re-checked. `break` and `continue` are only valid inside a
`while` body -- using either outside raises a runtime error.

```mlpl
# Count up to 5 (loop value is 0; i ends at 5).
i = 0
while i - 5 { i = i + 1 }

# Break with a value.
first_good = while 1 {
  x = next()
  if is_valid(x) { break x } else { 0 }
}

# Continue skips the s-update for i == 3.
i = 0
s = 0
while i - 5 {
  i = i + 1
  if i - 3 { 0 } else { continue }
  s = s + 1
}
```

Loops do not introduce a new scope: assignments in the body
persist in the surrounding environment, matching `repeat` /
`train` / `for` semantics.

### try / catch (error trap)

`try { body } catch e { handler }` is an EXPRESSION: it yields the
body's last value, or -- when the body raises a HARD error -- the
handler's, with `e` bound to the canonical error record
`{kind, message}` (dispatch on `e.kind`; kinds are stable kebab-case
tags like `shape`, `arity`, `runtime`). `err(...)` VALUES are data,
not hard errors: they flow through untouched. break/continue/return
signals also pass through. Design: docs/error-handling.md.

### `?` (Result propagation)

Postfix `?` (sugar for `check(expr)`): if the expression is `Ok(v)`,
continue with `v`; if `Err(e)`, EARLY-RETURN that whole Result from
the enclosing `def u:` function (the railway pattern). At top level
(no enclosing function) an `Err` is loud, like `unwrap`. Applying
`?` to a non-Result is an error.

## Array Display

## Broadcasting Rules

When an operator combines a scalar with an array, the scalar is
broadcast to match the array's shape:

```
[1, 2, 3] + 10     # [11, 12, 13]
5 * [1, 2, 3]       # [5, 10, 15]
```

When both operands are arrays, they must have the same shape.

## Error Handling

Errors are reported inline with descriptive messages:

# Lesson 01 -- Magmas, via Rock-Paper-Scissors.
#
# Meaning here: a MAGMA is a set with a closed binary operation.  Nothing else
# is assumed -- no associativity, no identity, no inverses, no order.
# Also called: "groupoid" in older algebra texts -- NOT the category-theory
# groupoid, which is a different object entirely.  See docs/terminology.md.
#
# fight(a, b) returns the winner; a tie returns the shared choice.  That is a
# closed binary operation on {rock, paper, scissors}, so it is a magma -- and
# this lesson shows it is nothing more than a magma.
#
# The same operation is shown three ways: as a function, as a Cayley table,
# and as a colored diagram.  They are one object seen from three sides.
#
# visual: ascii, svg
# loops: 0
# complexity: n^2 to build the table, n^3 to check associativity

include "lib/algebra.mlpl"
include "lib/render.mlpl"

names = ["rock", "paper", "scissors"]

# --- View 1: the operation as a function -----------------------------------
# rock 0 beats scissors 2, paper 1 beats rock 0, scissors 2 beats paper 1.
# The winner of a and b is whichever one the other does not beat.
def u:beats(x, y) { eq(mod(x - y + 3, 3), 1) }
def u:fight(x, y) { if u:beats(x, y) { x } else { y } }

# --- View 2: the same operation as a Cayley table ---------------------------
# table() is the outer product: every pair of choices, evaluated at once.
t = table(:u:fight, u:elements(3), u:elements(3))

u:show_table("Rock-Paper-Scissors as a magma", names, t)

# The function and the table agree by construction; assert it anyway.
spot = eq(u:fight(0, 2), take(take(t, 0, 0), 0, 2))

print("")
print("Which laws hold?")
u:show_laws(t)

# --- Closed, commutative, and nothing else ---------------------------------
# Closure is what makes this a magma at all: fight never invents a fourth
# choice.  Commutativity holds because the winner does not depend on which
# player moved first.  Associativity fails, and the failure is exhibited.
print("")
x = u:show_assoc_counterexample(names, t)

# --- View 3: the diagram ----------------------------------------------------
wrote = u:write_cayley_svg("out/01-rock-paper-scissors.svg",
  "Rock-Paper-Scissors (magma)", names, t)
print("")
print("wrote out/01-rock-paper-scissors.svg:", is_ok(wrote))

# --- Invariants -------------------------------------------------------------
c = u:classify(t)
if c.closed * c.commutative * (1 - c.associative) * (1 - c.identity)
   * spot * x.found * is_ok(wrote)
   * eq(x.a, 0) * eq(x.b, 1) * eq(x.c, 2) {
  ok("rock-paper-scissors is a commutative magma and no more")
} else {
  err("rock-paper-scissors invariants failed")
}

454-A script can reuse definitions from another local source file
455-with a top-level declaration:
456-
457-```text
458-include "vector.mlpl"
459-```
460-
461-- The path is one literal, relative path -- never computed,
462-  absolute, or conditional. `include` is only legal at the top
463-  level of a source file (not inside blocks or functions), and
464-  only in script mode: the browser session, connect mode, and
465-  interactive prompt answer it with a precise error instead.
466-- Included definitions (`u:` functions, bindings) enter the
467-  program at the include site, in source order.

469-  script.mlpl` roots all includes under DIR; without the flag

472-  that was broken.

474-  file loads once per program (repeats are no-ops), and an
475-  include cycle errors with the complete chain.

477-  file names that file and its own line and column.
